# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical Reading: Varga and Holm's Comment on the Halden Pilot

**Bottom line:** Sections 1–4 are a valuable, well-documented correction. They use the microdata to show that the Halden 23.4% figure was inflated by unrecorded attrition, generous manager ratings and a scheduled-hours denominator. But the Comment then overreaches in the opposite direction. Its claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is not shown by its own analysis. It also conflicts with the randomised Varden evidence that the authors cite selectively. Their corrected estimate of about 11% actually sits close to Varden's 12.5%.

## 1. The arithmetic mostly checks out, with one exception

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Table 2 rows | 95.1/0.8 = **+18.9%**; 98.4/0.859 = **+14.6%**; 95.4/0.861 = **+10.8%**. All correct. |
| Hours ratios | 34.6/40.3 = 0.859; 34.8/40.4 = 0.861. Both correct. |
| Real revenue | 1.014/1.041 = 0.974, so **−2.6%**. Correct. |
| Overstatements | Output by about 4 points (98.9 vs 95.1); hours by about 6 points (20% vs 14.1%). Correct. |

**The hours decomposition does not add up.** The Comment says actual hours rose above the 32 scheduled because of +0.7 hours a day on four days (2.8 hours) plus 1.6 hours logged on the day off. That gives 32 + 4.4 = **36.4 hours**, not the reported 34.6. Measured from the baseline daily average (40.3/5 = 8.06 hours), four longer days alone come to about 35.0 hours, before adding any day-off work. Something is inconsistent, perhaps the bases differ because of part-timers or staggered schedules. The authors should reconcile it, since this figure is the denominator for their main correction.

## 2. What the Comment establishes

- **The withdrawals were misreported.** If the microdata are right, seven of the nine "preparation phase" withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule began, and six cited workload or output. That is a material misstatement in the working paper, not just a limitation. It also corrects my earlier reading, where I accepted that the withdrawals came before the pilot.
- **Manager ratings ran high.** Ratings exceeded records in 19 of 23 organisations. The bias is systematic, though modest at about 4 points.
- **Actual hours fell much less than 20%.** Time-tracking data put the fall at about 14%, consistent with Varden's 13–17%.
- **Real revenue fell.** It confirms the inflation problem with the nominal revenue figure.
- **The sector claim fails.** It makes the same point as before: a gain in every sector is guaranteed whenever output stays above 80.

## 3. The abstract overstates what was corrected

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. But Table 2 corrects only **output and hours**. Attrition is not corrected at all. The 10.8% is still computed on survivors, and the missing nine organisations are never modelled or bounded.

A bounding exercise would have been informative, for example assuming the withdrawn organisations had output indices of 80–90. Without one, the effect of attrition is asserted, not measured.

## 4. The corrected subsets have problems the authors only partly acknowledge

- **No uncertainty is reported.** Every corrected figure rests on 17–27 organisations, with no confidence intervals or tests. The 19-of-23 comparison is also untested.
- **The subsets may be skewed.** The data note admits they are not random, but not the likely direction. Organisations with time-tracking software and formal output records are probably concentrated in software and professional services, which had the highest output in Halden. The 10.8% may not represent the pilot.
- **Some "records" are themselves inputs.** "Billable hours delivered" falls mechanically when hours are cut, so a record-based index built partly on it is biased downward. The authors treat the records as ground truth without checking which organisations used which kind.
- **The retail evidence is thin.** The −11.2% retail figure rests on three organisations.

## 5. The novelty argument is the weakest link, and it carries the conclusion

The move from "about 11% remains" to "entirely an artifact" rests on Section 6, which has four problems:

1. **Two data points.** It extrapolates linearly from energy readings at months three and six. Even taken at face value, the line reaches zero around **month 8.7**, not 10. And decay can level off, so a straight-line extrapolation is not justified.
2. **Energy is not output.** The argument assumes productivity tracks self-reported energy without showing it.
3. **The direct test was available but not run.** The Halden output index was completed **monthly**. The authors have the microdata and could have checked whether output per hour declined from month to month. That is the obvious test of a novelty effect, and it is absent.
4. **The burden of proof is applied unevenly.** "Six months cannot distinguish novelty from a durable effect" is correct. But that cuts both ways. It leaves the question open, and does not support the conclusion that the gain is "entirely" novelty. The authors require proof of durability while accepting their own claim on extrapolation alone.

## 6. The Varden evidence is used selectively

- The Comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." Yet it ignores Varden's **case-processing** result from the same randomised trial: **+12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4)**.
- That result already meets most of the Comment's own recommendations: randomisation, record-based output, actual hours and a control group. Selection, manager bias and the scheduled-hours denominator cannot explain it.
- The two corrected estimates **converge**: about 10.8% in the corrected Halden subset and 12.5% in randomised Varden. Independent designs agreeing on an 11–12% short-run gain is evidence *for* a real effect, at least over the short run.
- **Novelty could still matter in Varden.** Staff were unblinded and the trial ran nine months, so Varden's 24-month follow-up is the right test. But that is a reason for caution, not for "entirely".

## 7. The meetings section misrepresents Varden

- **Wrong on the facts.** It says the seven offices were "selected for analysis after the results were known." In Varden, the seven are *all* treated case-processing offices, not a chosen subgroup. The calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **Ignores the safeguards.** Varden labelled the analysis exploratory, listed its limits and registered a confirmatory test. The Comment mentions none of this.
- **Misses the real flaw.** As noted earlier, there were no baseline meeting data, so "offices that cut meetings most" cannot have been measured. The Comment's criticism should have been this.
- **Conflicts with the novelty argument.** If the meetings mechanism is real, removing low-value time would produce a *durable* gain. That may be why the Comment is keen to dismiss it.

## 8. Overall assessment

| Claim | Support |
|---|---|
| Halden's 23.4% is substantially overstated | **Strong** |
| Halden misreported its withdrawals | **Strong**, if the microdata are as described |
| Corrected gain is about 11% in the usable subset | **Moderate.** Small, non-random subset; no uncertainty; hours decomposition unreconciled |
| Reduced hours cut output in coverage-bound work | **Moderate–strong**, mainly because of Varden |
| The remaining gain is novelty | **Weak.** Speculative, and the direct test was available but not run |
| Per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" | **Not supported.** Contradicted by Varden's case-processing result |

The Comment repeats the error it criticises. Halden turned its data into a sweeping claim that the model works in every sector. Varga and Holm turn a good correction into a sweeping claim that the gains are entirely artifact.

The defensible synthesis across all three documents is narrower:
- Short-run per-hour gains of roughly 10–12% appear in work where output is not tied to presence.
- Work that depends on presence loses output and service.
- Whether the gains last is an open question, which Varden's 24-month follow-up is placed to answer.
